title: LRU Cache
keyIdea: Hash map key → node + doubly linked list ordered by use (head side = most recent, tail side = least recent). get/put move the key's node to the front; when full, evict the node before tail. Dummy head/tail remove edge cases. Every operation is O(1).

approaches.name: Your old solution (map + list)
approaches.idea: Same structure. Updating a key unlinks the old node and inserts a new one; unlinked nodes are never deleted.
approaches.why: Correct and O(1), but leaks a node on every update and every eviction.

approaches.name: std::list + splice
approaches.idea: list<pair<key,value>> in use order; map key → iterator. splice moves to the front, pop_back evicts.
approaches.why: Same design using the standard library, no manual memory.

approaches.name: Map + doubly linked list (clean)
approaches.idea: unlink + pushFront helpers. Existing key: update val in place and move to front. Full: unlink tail->prev, erase its key, delete it.
approaches.why: A few pointer changes and one map operation per call; no wasted or leaked nodes.

quiz.q: Why do you need both a hash map and a linked list?
options: The map finds a key's node in O(1); the list keeps use order and moves/evicts in O(1)
The map is for values only
The list is for sorting keys

quiz.q: Why must each node store its key?
options: On eviction you only have tail->prev, and you need its key to erase it from the map

quiz.q: What did the old solution do wrong?
options: Removed nodes were unlinked but never deleted (a memory leak), and updates made a new node

quiz.q: Why use dummy head and tail nodes?
options: Every real node always has a prev and next, so no NULL checks when linking/unlinking
To make it faster than O(1)
Yes: the key becomes most recently used, so its node moves to the front
Only if the key is missing
